What are we here for?

The dataset: World of Warcraft Avatar history Dataset 1

World of Warcraft is a subscription-based online videogame.




The problem: Some players eventually stop playing, and thus stop paying their subscription.

Our “unit of analysis” is a (player character, month) pair.

title: Part 5 · Assembling the plan, and running it
text:
Everything so far has been a function that takes a table and returns a table. A skrub Data Op is what turns those functions into a plan: a graph of nodes, each one either a step of the pre-processing or the estimator at the end, with the hyperparameters declared alongside so that they can be tuned together.








Tip





Loading and downsampling the file (click to expand)
load parses the raw .txt heartbeat logs itself — parsing is a node of the plan, not a separate pre-processing script — then downsamples the result to reduce execution time. We need to be deliberate with how we sample the data: rather than choosing a random subset of the values in the dataset, we need to be careful to select a subset of characters and keep all the rows for those characters. This ensures that we have reliable information about all the characters.


def load(file_paths, fraction=0.1):
    """Parse the given raw ".txt" log files, then subsample by character."""
    df = parse_files(file_paths)
    if fraction == 1:
        return df.lazy()

    df = sample_by_user(df, fraction=fraction)
    return df.lazy()





Sampling by character rather than by row is not a detail. A row-level sample would punch holes in each character’s monthly timeline, and a character with a missing month looks exactly like a character who churned — the label would be corrupted by the sampling. Keeping every row of a smaller set of characters costs the same in compute and leaves the timelines intact.



load parses first and samples second, and the sampling is one line of polars: take the distinct char values, draw a fraction of them, keep every row whose char is in that set. The default fraction is 0.1, and --fraction 1 skips the sampling entirely. The draw is seeded (seed=42), so the same characters come back on every run — the model is not seeded, but the sample is.
The obvious alternative is to sample rows, and it is wrong here in a way that is easy to miss, because the table it produces looks perfectly reasonable. It has the same number of rows, the same columns, and no nulls. What it does not have is intact timelines.






A 10% sample of the rows, for 40 characters drawn at random from the 20,472 the sample kept. Blue: the sample kept the month. Orange: the character played that month, but the sample dropped it. Grey: the character did not play.

The orange blocks are the problem. Each one is a month the character demonstrably played, which the row sample threw away. Nothing about the character changed — only how the sample was drawn.
The damage is not marginal. On the 2008 table — 10.8M heartbeats, 37,354 characters, 98,972 character-months — a 10% row sample keeps 20,472 characters but loses 24% of the character-months those characters actually played. Of those characters, 13.9% end up with a hole in the middle of their timeline, 1.85 months wide on average. A character-level sample of the same size keeps 3,735 characters and loses nothing.
The holes matter because of how the label is built. has_played is derived from presence in the table, so a dropped month is indistinguishable from a month the character did not play. churn is “absent this month and the previous one”, so a dropped month can flip a row from negative to positive. Measured on the same 2008 data, 33% of the positives in the row-level sample are spurious — 5,519 of 16,701 — while no true positive is lost. The corruption is one-directional: it only invents churners, never hides them. Precision against the true labels is 0.67 and recall is 1.0.
That asymmetry is the reason the choice is not a matter of taste. A model trained on the row sample would be learning to predict the sampling pattern as much as the behaviour, and the pattern is not random with respect to the target: it fires exactly on the rows where a character played a little. The character-level sample costs the same to parse (the parse happens before the sample) and about the same to fit (1.08M rows against 1.12M), and it buys complete timelines for fewer characters instead of broken timelines for more.
The same load node runs on the held-out files, so the unseen evaluation samples 10% of the characters of the unseen window, not the characters chosen for training. That is deliberate: the held-out run should not be able to recognise which characters the model was fitted on.



The hyperparameters of the pipeline are declared with skrub’s choose_* functions. They fall into three groups, and the grouping is what decides how they can be searched:

Feature-table choices change the arguments of build_feature_table, so each distinct combination is a separate entry in the skrub cache and a full rebuild of the feature table: the session gap, the zone-session gap, how many lags and diffs to add, whether to use location features, the Gini coefficient, and whether to add the monthly and class-level blocks.
Structural choices only change what happens after the feature table is built, so a trial costs one refit per fold: whether to drop char and month, the vectorizer’s cardinality threshold, its high-cardinality encoder, its null-drop fraction, and the regularisation of the linear model.
Capacity choices are the model’s own hyperparameters: the learning rate, the number of leaves, the minimum samples per leaf and the L2 penalty.

Mixing the first group into a model search would make most trials pay for a feature-table rebuild they do not need, so the search runs in stages: a coarse search over the feature choices on a 2% sample, then the structural choices with a logistic regression, then the capacity choices with the gradient-boosted model. make_data_op(stage=...) declares only the group a stage is meant to explore; frozen= carries the winner of one stage into the next.






Tip



Full Data Op construction script


def make_data_op(load_fraction=0.1, return_x=False):
    raw_files = skrub.var("raw_files")
    # Parsing the raw logs is a node of the plan like any other: the exact
    # same code path parses whichever files the "raw_files" environment
    # variable points to, whether that's the historical training set or a
    # held-out, never-before-seen set of files.
    historical_data = raw_files.skb.apply_func(load, fraction=load_fraction)
    # In the original data, "guild == -1" means "no guild", so I'm replacing -1
    # with nulls.
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("guild") == -1)
        .then(None)
        .otherwise(pl.col("guild"))
        .alias("guild")
    )

    # Only score characters that played in the previous month: the others have
    # no features to predict from.
    user_month_has_played = historical_data.skb.apply_func(
        build_churn_dataset, only_prev_active=True
    ).skb.set_name("query")
    X = user_month_has_played["char", "month"].skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter())
    y = user_month_has_played["churn_next"].skb.mark_as_y()

    # Hyperparameters
    session_gap = skrub.choose_from([30, 60, 15], name="session_gap")
    use_location = skrub.choose_bool(name="location_features")
    lags = skrub.choose_from(
        {"no": None, "1": (1,), "1_2": (1, 2), "1_2_3": (1, 2, 3)}, name="lags"
    )

    # Built from the full historical data (a plain, non-X node), independent of
    # the CV fold split of X, so lagged features always see each character's
    # complete monthly timeline regardless of which fold is being evaluated.
    feature_table = historical_data.collect().skb.apply_func(
        build_feature_table,
        session_gap=session_gap,
        use_location=use_location,
        # The Gini coefficient is off: measured against the pipeline's own
        # time-based splitter it adds nothing over the rarity and zone-level
        # columns, and it costs 1.4s of the 1.6s location block.
        add_gini=False,
        lags=lags,
        _fingerprint=FEATURES_FINGERPRINT,
    )
    all_features = X.skb.apply_func(add_features, feature_table)
    encoded = all_features.skb.apply(skrub.TableVectorizer())
    data_op = encoded.skb.apply(
        HGB(learning_rate=skrub.choose_float(0.1, 0.5, log=True)), y=y
    ).skb.with_scoring("roc_auc")
    # data_op = encoded.skb.apply(DummyClassifier(), y=y) #.skb.with_scoring("roc_auc")
    if return_x:
        return data_op, X
    return data_op







The plan ends in a TableVectorizer followed by a HistGradientBoostingClassifier. The vectorizer is what makes the mixed table usable: it one-hot encodes the low-cardinality categorical columns (race, class, most frequent zone, guilds) and leaves the numeric and duration columns alone. The gradient-boosted tree model is a good fit for the rest — it handles nulls natively, needs no scaling, and picks up the non-linearities in features like level and session count without any manual binning.
The structural choices are searched with a logistic regression rather than the gradient-boosted model. That is a statistical choice, not a speed one: with the cache warm the feature table is free, so a trial costs 30 folds of vectorizer plus model fitting either way. A linear model has far fewer effective parameters, so the effect of dropping char or changing the cardinality threshold is readable from the results instead of being buried in the variance of a large tree ensemble. The linear branch needs a median imputer (the lag columns are null for a character’s first months) and skrub’s SquashingScaler, which is what tabular_pipeline uses for linear models.
char is exposed as a choice rather than dropped outright. It is an identifier, not a feature, and left in the model can memorise per-character behaviour that will not exist for a new character — but the search should show that rather than have it asserted.
The scoring function is roc_auc. Accuracy would be misleading here, because churn_next is true for only about 36.5% of the rows in the 2008 churn dataset (81,199 rows over 10 months), so a model that always predicts “not churned” already scores 0.64 accuracy while ranking nothing. AUC 0.5 is genuine chance, and that is the number to compare against.



The plan scores only characters that played in the previous month (only_prev_active=True). The alternative — keeping every row, including characters who were already absent — gives 221,237 rows in the 2008 data with 54.5% positives, against 81,199 rows and 36.5% positives for the restricted version.
The restricted version is not just smaller, it is easier to score well on. 75% of the old positive rows were already absent in the previous month, so the trivial rule “absent last month” gets ROC AUC 0.63 without any model at all. On the same test rows, a model trained on all rows scores 0.64 to 0.82 depending on the month, against 0.82 to 0.90 when trained on active rows only. The rows with no features do not make the problem easier — they pollute training. The cause is not tested here, but the direction is consistent across every month.
There is also an operational argument: you can only retain characters who are still around. Scoring characters who have already left produces a number that looks like a churn rate but cannot be acted on.

The holes matter because of how the label is built. has_played is derived from presence in the table, so a dropped month is indistinguishable from a month the character did not play. churn is “absent this month and the previous one”, so a dropped month can flip a row from negative to positive. Measured on the same 2008 data, 33% of the positives in the row-level sample are spurious — 5,519 of 16,701 — while no true positive is lost. The corruption is one-directional: it only invents churners, never hides them. Precision against the true labels is 0.67 and recall is 1.0.
That asymmetry is the reason the choice is not a matter of taste. A model trained on the row sample would be learning to predict the sampling pattern as much as the behaviour, and the pattern is not random with respect to the target: it fires exactly on the rows where a character played a little. The character-level sample costs the same to parse (the parse happens before the sample) and about the same to fit (1.08M rows against 1.12M), and it buys complete timelines for fewer characters instead of broken timelines for more.
The same load node runs on the held-out files, so the unseen evaluation samples 10% of the characters of the unseen window, not the characters chosen for training. That is deliberate: the held-out run should not be able to recognise which characters the model was fitted on.



The hyperparameters of the pipeline are declared with skrub’s choose_* functions. They fall into three groups, and the grouping is what decides how they can be searched:

Feature-table choices change the arguments of build_feature_table, so each distinct combination is a separate entry in the skrub cache and a full rebuild of the feature table: the session gap, the zone-session gap, how many lags and diffs to add, whether to use location features, the Gini coefficient, and whether to add the monthly and class-level blocks.
Structural choices only change what happens after the feature table is built, so a trial costs one refit per fold: whether to drop char and month, the vectorizer’s cardinality threshold, its high-cardinality encoder, its null-drop fraction, and the regularisation of the linear model.
Capacity choices are the model’s own hyperparameters: the learning rate, the number of leaves, the minimum samples per leaf and the L2 penalty.

Mixing the first group into a model search would make most trials pay for a feature-table rebuild they do not need, so the search runs in stages: a coarse search over the feature choices on a 2% sample, then the structural choices with a logistic regression, then the capacity choices with the gradient-boosted model. make_data_op(stage=...) declares only the group a stage is meant to explore; frozen= carries the winner of one stage into the next.






Tip



Full Data Op construction script


def make_data_op(load_fraction=0.1, return_x=False):
    raw_files = skrub.var("raw_files")
    # Parsing the raw logs is a node of the plan like any other: the exact
    # same code path parses whichever files the "raw_files" environment
    # variable points to, whether that's the historical training set or a
    # held-out, never-before-seen set of files.
    historical_data = raw_files.skb.apply_func(load, fraction=load_fraction)
    # In the original data, "guild == -1" means "no guild", so I'm replacing -1
    # with nulls.
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("guild") == -1)
        .then(None)
        .otherwise(pl.col("guild"))
        .alias("guild")
    )

    # Only score characters that played in the previous month: the others have
    # no features to predict from.
    user_month_has_played = historical_data.skb.apply_func(
        build_churn_dataset, only_prev_active=True
    ).skb.set_name("query")
    X = user_month_has_played["char", "month"].skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter())
    y = user_month_has_played["churn_next"].skb.mark_as_y()

    # Hyperparameters
    session_gap = skrub.choose_from([30, 60, 15], name="session_gap")
    use_location = skrub.choose_bool(name="location_features")
    lags = skrub.choose_from(
        {"no": None, "1": (1,), "1_2": (1, 2), "1_2_3": (1, 2, 3)}, name="lags"
    )

    # Built from the full historical data (a plain, non-X node), independent of
    # the CV fold split of X, so lagged features always see each character's
    # complete monthly timeline regardless of which fold is being evaluated.
    feature_table = historical_data.collect().skb.apply_func(
        build_feature_table,
        session_gap=session_gap,
        use_location=use_location,
        # The Gini coefficient is off: measured against the pipeline's own
        # time-based splitter it adds nothing over the rarity and zone-level
        # columns, and it costs 1.4s of the 1.6s location block.
        add_gini=False,
        lags=lags,
        _fingerprint=FEATURES_FINGERPRINT,
    )
    all_features = X.skb.apply_func(add_features, feature_table)
    encoded = all_features.skb.apply(skrub.TableVectorizer())
    data_op = encoded.skb.apply(
        HGB(learning_rate=skrub.choose_float(0.1, 0.5, log=True)), y=y
    ).skb.with_scoring("roc_auc")
    # data_op = encoded.skb.apply(DummyClassifier(), y=y) #.skb.with_scoring("roc_auc")
    if return_x:
        return data_op, X
    return data_op







The plan ends in a TableVectorizer followed by a HistGradientBoostingClassifier. The vectorizer is what makes the mixed table usable: it one-hot encodes the low-cardinality categorical columns (race, class, most frequent zone, guilds) and leaves the numeric and duration columns alone. The gradient-boosted tree model is a good fit for the rest — it handles nulls natively, needs no scaling, and picks up the non-linearities in features like level and session count without any manual binning.
The structural choices are searched with a logistic regression rather than the gradient-boosted model. That is a statistical choice, not a speed one: with the cache warm the feature table is free, so a trial costs 30 folds of vectorizer plus model fitting either way. A linear model has far fewer effective parameters, so the effect of dropping char or changing the cardinality threshold is readable from the results instead of being buried in the variance of a large tree ensemble. The linear branch needs a median imputer (the lag columns are null for a character’s first months) and skrub’s SquashingScaler, which is what tabular_pipeline uses for linear models.
char is exposed as a choice rather than dropped outright. It is an identifier, not a feature, and left in the model can memorise per-character behaviour that will not exist for a new character — but the search should show that rather than have it asserted.
The scoring function is roc_auc. Accuracy would be misleading here, because churn_next is true for only about 36.5% of the rows in the 2008 churn dataset (81,199 rows over 10 months), so a model that always predicts “not churned” already scores 0.64 accuracy while ranking nothing. AUC 0.5 is genuine chance, and that is the number to compare against.



The plan scores only characters that played in the previous month (only_prev_active=True). The alternative — keeping every row, including characters who were already absent — gives 221,237 rows in the 2008 data with 54.5% positives, against 81,199 rows and 36.5% positives for the restricted version.
The restricted version is not just smaller, it is easier to score well on. 75% of the old positive rows were already absent in the previous month, so the trivial rule “absent last month” gets ROC AUC 0.63 without any model at all. On the same test rows, a model trained on all rows scores 0.64 to 0.82 depending on the month, against 0.82 to 0.90 when trained on active rows only. The rows with no features do not make the problem easier — they pollute training. The cause is not tested here, but the direction is consistent across every month.
There is also an operational argument: you can only retain characters who are still around. Scoring characters who have already left produces a number that looks like a churn rate but cannot be acted on.

2 Running it
The data op is evaluated by passing a list of raw log file paths as input — parsing them is itself one of the plan’s nodes (see “Loading and downsampling the file” above). Here we cross-validate it on 10% of the characters of the historical (through October 2008) files:

data_op = make_data_op(load_fraction=0.1)
results = data_op.skb.cross_validate(environment=main.get_env("train"))







Note



Only characters that played in the previous month are scored (see only_prev_active=True above): the characters that were already absent have no features and are not the ones that could be retained, and keeping them in the training set lowers the scores on the characters that are still active.

3 Tuning
random_search wraps the plan in an Optuna study, persisted to wowah_churn_study.db so that a run can be resumed. Two settings matter more than the search space itself:

study_name. Without it skrub generates a fresh UUID per call, which is why the database accumulated six studies before this was fixed.
The search is sequential, and that is not a default to be raised. Parsing is a node of the plan and it spawns a process pool sized to the core count, so N parallel trials on a cold cache means N × cores processes. Measured at a 2% sample: 2 workers gave a 1.4× speedup and 4 gave 2.6×, but 8 drove a 24 GB machine into 40 GB of swap. The earlier n_jobs=-1 runs are the same failure in a different guise — 72 failed trials, every one with location_features=1, all dying within nine seconds of starting.
timeout is safe precisely because the search is sequential. skrub switches to Optuna’s threaded parallelisation only when a timeout is set and n_jobs > 1, and threads deadlock against the parser’s process pool. Note that a timeout counts wall-clock time, so a sleeping machine burns it; n_iter is the more predictable bound.

text:
2 Sessions
We first need to define what a “session” is in this context.
The reason we need sessions is because we have access to heartbeats, which only tell us that the avatar was online at the time of the poll. They do not give us unformation about when the player logged in, logged out, or how many sittings a player had through a month.
We use the SessionEncoder to add a “session ID” feature to the feature matrix, which is then used as the base feature for all the other session features.

2.1 The rule






Important



A session is a run of heartbeats in which consecutive beats are at most session_gap apart. One character’s beats are sorted by time, the gap to the previous beat is computed, and every gap larger than the threshold opens a new session.


session_encoder = SessionEncoder(
    split_by="char", timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap * 60
)
beats = session_encoder.fit_transform(month_of_heartbeats)
The SessionEncoder is stateless: its functionality is limited to adding a column (timestamp_session_id) to each row, while keeping the other values and the row order unchanged. This also means that the encoder needs to be refit for each month: sessions are a property of the data, rather than a fixed transformation.


2.2 Choosing the session gap
Given that polls are executed with a ten-minutes cadence (with some variance), a gap of 10 minutes is expected of all players and thus does not mean anything; a gap of multiple hours instead means that the player took a break.
The actual value is a modelling decision that can be tuned along all other hyperparameters thanks to the skrub choices:
session_gap = skrub.choose_from([30, 45, 60], name="session_gap")
15 minutes is deliberately not offered. Heartbeats arrive roughly every ten minutes, so a 15-minute threshold splits a session whenever a single poll is missed: only 53.8% of gaps are at most 10 minutes, so the threshold would be cutting through the middle of the distribution rather than separating “still playing” from “took a break”. At 30 minutes 91.1% of gaps stay inside a session, and at 60 minutes 92.0%.
The zone-level encoder has its own gap (zone_session_gap), because how long a character stayed in one zone is a different process from how long they played. "same" reuses session_gap, which is the historical behaviour.
On the 2008 data, the vast majority (83.6%) of consecutive-heartbeat gaps are within 15 minutes, while 91.0% of the gaps are within 60. Their effect on the features is real but not dramatic: over March 2008 a character-month has a median of 4 sessions at any of the three gaps, and the mean falls from 15.2 at 15 minutes to 12.0 at 60.

text:
3 The loop that builds the table






Full feature engineering function (click to expand)


def filter_df_by_month(df, month):
    return df.filter(pl.col("month") == month)


def build_feature_table(
    historical_data,
    session_gap=30,
    use_location=True,
    add_gini=False,
    interval="1mo",
    lags=(1, 2),
    _fingerprint=None,
):
    """
    Build the feature table for every (char, month) pair.

    This function makes sure that we are only ever using historical data up to
    the given month - 1 month. This is to avoid any leakage in the data.

    It builds the table for every (char, month) pair a character could appear
    in (not just the rows asked for by a given CV fold), because lagged
    features need each character's full monthly timeline: a CV fold's X may
    contain a single month (e.g. the test fold), which would otherwise leave
    every lag/diff column null.

    `_fingerprint` is unused; it only exists so that the cache key changes when
    the code this function calls into changes (see `FEATURES_FINGERPRINT`).
    """
    del _fingerprint
    features_by_month = []

    # Create a session encoder. The gap is a hyperparameter that can be tuned.
    # This encoder is used as a stateless transformer so it is refitted for every
    # month
    session_encoder = SessionEncoder(
        split_by="char", timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap * 60
    )
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval)
    ).lazy()

    # Every (char, month) pair a character could appear in, whether or not they
    # played that month: the full grid lag/diff features are built over.
    user_month = build_churn_dataset(historical_data).select("char", "month").lazy()
    # Adding fixed features: these features are fixed by character so they don't
    # change over time.
    user_month = user_month.join(
        historical_data.select("char", "race", "charclass").unique("char"),
        on="char",
        how="left",
        maintain_order="left",
    ).collect()

    # This is used to add the historical data up to the given month.
    # Sorting months is not needed, but forces a consistent order (better for debugging)
    for month in user_month["month"].unique().sort():
        this_month_X = filter_df_by_month(user_month, month)

        # Selecting only the entries in the historical data from the month before
        # the one I am building features for.
        # This means that if the row's month is April, then the historical data
        # is filtered to keep only the rows from March. Shifting the data forward
        # by one interval and filtering on the current month is equivalent to
        # saying "I want the rows for the current month - 1 month", but it's
        # easier to implement
        kept_historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
            pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(interval)
        ).filter(pl.col("month") == month)

        # Session features: a session starts from a heartbeat, then it ends when
        # no more heartbeats are detected for session_gap minutes
        historical_data_sessions = session_encoder.fit_transform(
            kept_historical_data.collect()
        ).lazy()
        historical_data_sessions = get_session_duration(historical_data_sessions)

        # General features: add session based and playerbase features
        df_with_features = add_general_features(
            this_month_X.lazy(), historical_data_sessions
        )

        # Location features can be useful but take much longer to generate
        if use_location:
            # Grouping by character and zone so that I can get the time spent in each zone
            # Even if users leave the zone, this lets me find how much time a user spends in
            # a given zone
            session_encoder_zone = SessionEncoder(
                split_by=["char", "zone"],
                timestamp_col="timestamp",
                session_gap=session_gap * 60,
                suffix="session_id_zone",
            )
            # Zone-session features: a session lasts from the first time a character
            # enters a zone to the moment it leaves it
            # This is useful to get zone-specific features
            historical_data_zone_sessions = session_encoder_zone.fit_transform(
                kept_historical_data.collect()
            ).lazy()
            historical_data_zone_sessions = get_session_duration(
                historical_data_zone_sessions,
                session_column="timestamp_session_id_zone",
            )
            df_with_features = add_location_features(
                df_with_features,
                historical_data_zone_sessions,
                add_gini=add_gini,
            )
        else:
            df_with_features = df_with_features.collect()
        features_by_month.append(df_with_features)
        assert len(df_with_features) == len(this_month_X)

    feature_table = pl.concat(features_by_month, how="vertical")
    to_fill = pl.col("monthly_total_session_duration", "monthly_avg_session_duration")
    feature_table = feature_table.with_columns(
        to_fill.fill_null(pl.duration(seconds=0))
    )
    if lags is not None:
        feature_table = add_lagged_features(feature_table, lags=lags)
    return feature_table


def add_features(X, feature_table):
    """Attach this CV fold's (char, month) rows to the precomputed features."""
    return X.join(
        feature_table, on=["char", "month"], how="left", maintain_order="left"
    )





The next part takes the optional block on the list — location features — and asks whether it earns its place.

title: Part 1 · The dataset
text:
We rely on the World of Warcraft Avatar History dataset. The dataset is built by scanning the game’s Taiwanese server roughly every 10 minutes, and logging information about each user character in the Horde faction that is found online at the timestamp’s time. As we have a sequence of timestamps, this lets us track the behavior of players over time.
The dataset spans roughly 3 years, with the first timestamps being recorded on 2005-12-31 and the final on 2009-01-10. This time frame includes the release of two expansions, The Burning Crusade and Wrath of the Lich King: expansions are major events in the dataset, as they introduce new content and bring a major influx of new and old players.






Note





Expansion dates and Taiwanese release
WoWAH was collected on the Taiwanese server Light’s Hope, so it follows the Taiwan/Hong Kong release schedule rather than the North American/European one: importantly the first expansion (The Burning Crusade) launched in April 2007 rather than in January; the second expansion (Wrath of the Lich King) released in November 2008 in both cases.





Through this write-up, we will use the terms “character” and “avatar” interchangeably: both terms will be used to refer to any single player-controlled character that is found online when the server snapshot is taken.
Avatar information includes:

The avatar’s ID (a unique integer ID for anonymization)

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
In this post we will see how we can predict player churn in World of Warcraft (WoW), a subscription-based MMORPG released in 2004. More precisely, we are interested in predicting a player’s behavior in a given month, and decide whether there is a risk that they will stop playing the next month.
To do so, we want to train a machine learning model that, given features based on each player’s behavior and on the overall playerbase, will be able to predict whether player X will stop playing in a given month.
To keep the focus of this post on the process rather than the code, most of the lower-level functions will be hidden in collapsible blocks, including much of the pre-processing and feature engineering. The entire code is available in this repository.

The post is split into parts, each one short enough to read on its own:

The dataset — what the heartbeat logs are, how they are parsed, and a first look at the table.

title: Part 2 · What churn means here, and a splitter that respects time
text:
Modeling user churn is a common application of machine learning models, though the definition of churn is typically business-specific. In general, by “user churn” one refers to “a user that does not come back to the service for a certain length of time, if ever”.
In the context of this example, churn refers to those avatars that are not found online for at least two consecutive months: we consider those characters as users that stopped playing, and consequently suspended their subscription.






Important



In WoW, a single player may have multiple “player characters” or “avatars”. The information available in the dataset does not allow us to link a player to their avatars, and as such we will treat each avatar as an independent player.
This is reflected in how we model churn: as we do not have access to which player is behind each avatar, we assume that any churned avatar is a churned player.


As we do not have access to the actual subscription data, we assume that a player has suspended their subscription when they stop playing for two consecutive months. A single missing month is more likely a break than a cancellation, so a character that skips a month and then comes back is not considered churned.
For this post, we aggregate player behaviors at a monthly basis, and add a has_played flag that tells us if a player has played at least once during each month. From it, we derive two columns:

churn: the character has churned as of this month, i.e., has_played is False both in this month and in the previous one.
churn_next: the value of churn in the following month. This is the target that we want to predict.







Important



Our objective
Given a month (e.g., June), we want to use all the data up to the last day of the previous month (all months until May included) to predict whether a user will have churned as of July (i.e., their has_played flag will be False both in June and in July).
In other words, a row at month M means “act during month M, using data up to the end of M-1, to predict absence in M and M+1.”









Warning



Why we’re predicting one month in the future
Given the month of June, we may be tempted to use churn at this month as the target. However, June’s features are built from May, and churn for June is only true if the character is absent in May: any character that is active in May is labeled as “not churned” by construction, and the model would learn that just by looking at the missing values. This would produce overly optimistic results.
Shifting the target to July avoids this problem: in June we want to predict whether a player is active in July using data from and up to May.


One caveat with this modeling strategy is that we are working with historical data, so we cannot actually apply said incentive and observe whether it has an impact like in a typical A/B test.


We begin by adding two columns to the historical dataset: in the first we store each timestamp, truncated to have a monthly resolution; in the second we track the first month for each character. Additionally, we add a constant has_played column that acts as our “player was seen” flag.
We are interested in monthly snapshots, so the dataset is then reduced to select only the unique (character, month) pairs.






Data preparation


def make_data(df, interval="1mo"):
    """
    Prepare a dataframe that contains the months in which each player has
    actually played. The column "has_played" is then set to True for those months.
    Any month in which the player did not play is missing from this dataset,
    because the dataset is built starting from player activity, so any "empty
    month" simply doesn't exist in this dataset.
    """

    data = (
        df.with_columns(
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).alias("month"),
            first_month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).min().over("char"),
        )
        .unique(subset=["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(pl.lit(True).alias("has_played"))
    )
    return data

Since we want to predict the behavior a player will have over a single month, our target variable will be grouped by “user-month” (e.g., ID153_2026-12). However, not all players will play at least once every month, so by relying exclusively on the historical data we would be missing samples; to get around this problem we generate a char_month dataset that contains all unique combinations of users and months by executing the cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.







Cross product
The cross product between two sets (in this case, months and unique users) builds a new set where each element in the first set is paired with all elements in the second set.

def make_user_month(df, interval="1mo"):
    """
    Create a DataFrame with all unique combinations of users and months.
    This will be used to ensure that we have a row for each user for each month
    in the range of the dataset, even if the user did not play in that month.

    This is done with a cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.

    This function is artificially generating 3 months past the last month in the
    dataset. Their "churn_next" is null, so `build_churn_dataset` drops them: they
    are only visible when calling `add_churn` directly.

    Note that since the months are generated from the range of the dataset, they
    may include months prior to a user's first activity. These will need to be
    filtered out later.
    """

    months = pl.datetime_range(
        start=df.select(pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).min())
        .collect()
        .item(),
        end=df.select(
            # Adding 3 months to the end of the range because we are adding
            # lagged features up to 3 months.
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).max().dt.offset_by("3mo")
        )
        .collect()
        .item(),
        interval=interval,
        closed="both",
        eager=True,
    )

    char_month = (
        df.with_columns(month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval))
        .select("char")
        .unique()
        .join(months.to_frame(name="month").lazy(), how="cross")
    )
    return char_month

The grid extends three months past the end of the data to make sure the learner does not crash with unseen data.
Now that we have all the combinations (character, month), we can join back the prepared data to mark all the months in which each character was found online, and marking all others with has_played=False.
Additionally, the resulting rows are filtered to remove all pairs (char, month) whose month precedes the character’s first month. We should not have a row about a character’s playtime in January if they started playing in August!
Then we add the churn information. After sorting by month, prev_played is the has_played flag of the previous month for the same character (False for the first month), churn marks the characters absent in both months, and churn_next is churn shifted one month back within each character. The last observed month has no “next month” to look at, so its churn_next is left empty, and so is that of the three padding months.






Add the churn columns


def add_churn(user_month, data):
    """
    Add churn information to the user-month DataFrame by merging it with the actual
    play data. The resulting DataFrame will have a "has_played" column indicating
    whether the user played in that month. Any missing values in "has_played" are
    filled with False: missing values mean that the player did not play in that
    particular month.

    It also adds the "churn" column (churned as of this month: absent this month
    and the previous one) and the "churn_next" column, the prediction target:
    the value of "churn" in the *following* month. Features for a given month are
    built from the previous month's data, so the target cannot be the churn
    status of the same month: that status includes "absent last month", which
    is exactly what the features reveal. "churn_next" is null for the last
    observed month and for the padding months added by `make_user_month`,
    because the following month has not been observed.
    """

    last_month = data.lazy().select(pl.col("month").max()).collect().item()

    df_with_user_month = (
        user_month.join(
            data,
            on=["char", "month"],
            how="left",
        )
        .with_columns(pl.col("has_played").fill_null(False))
        .with_columns(first_month=pl.col("first_month").min().over("char"))
        .filter(pl.col("first_month") <= pl.col("month"))
        .select(
            "char",
            "month",
            "has_played",
            "first_month",
        )
        .sort(["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(
            # has_played in the previous month for this character
            prev_played=pl.col("has_played").shift(1).over("char").fill_null(False)
        )
        .with_columns(
            # churn = absent this month AND absent last month
            # prev_played is False on a character's first month
            churn=~pl.col("has_played") & ~pl.col("prev_played")
        )
        .with_columns(
            churn_next=pl.when(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo") <= last_month)
            .then(pl.col("churn").shift(-1).over("char"))
            .otherwise(None)
        )
        .select(
            "char",
            "month",
            "has_played",
            "prev_played",
            "churn",
            "churn_next",
            "first_month",
        )
    )
    return df_with_user_month

Rows without a target are dropped, since they can be used neither for training nor for evaluation. def build_churn_dataset(historical_data, only_prev_active=False):
    """
    Build the (char, month) table with `has_played`, `prev_played`, `churn` and
    the target `churn_next`.

    Rows whose target is unknown (the last observed month and the padding months
    after it) cannot be used to train or evaluate a model, so they are dropped.

    With `only_prev_active=True`, only the rows where the character played in the
    previous month are kept. Features for a row at month M are built from month
    M - 1, so a character that was already absent in M - 1 has no features and
    is not a prediction we could act on: the target then only contains
    characters that were active in M - 1 and are absent in both M and M + 1.
    Keep the default (all rows) when the full (char, month) grid is needed, for
    example to build lagged features, which need each character's full timeline.
    """
    # Load the dataset
    data = make_data(historical_data)
    # Add the combinations of user months
    user_month = make_user_month(historical_data)
    churn_data = add_churn(user_month, data).filter(
        pl.col("churn_next").is_not_null()
    )
    if only_prev_active:
        churn_data = churn_data.filter(pl.col("prev_played"))
    return churn_data.collect()

title: Part 2 · What churn means here, and a splitter that respects time
text:
Modeling user churn is a common application of machine learning models, though the definition of churn is typically business-specific. In general, by “user churn” one refers to “a user that does not come back to the service for a certain length of time, if ever”.
In the context of this example, churn refers to those avatars that are not found online for at least two consecutive months: we consider those characters as users that stopped playing, and consequently suspended their subscription.






Important



In WoW, a single player may have multiple “player characters” or “avatars”. The information available in the dataset does not allow us to link a player to their avatars, and as such we will treat each avatar as an independent player.
This is reflected in how we model churn: as we do not have access to which player is behind each avatar, we assume that any churned avatar is a churned player.


As we do not have access to the actual subscription data, we assume that a player has suspended their subscription when they stop playing for two consecutive months. A single missing month is more likely a break than a cancellation, so a character that skips a month and then comes back is not considered churned.
For this post, we aggregate player behaviors at a monthly basis, and add a has_played flag that tells us if a player has played at least once during each month. From it, we derive two columns:

churn: the character has churned as of this month, i.e., has_played is False both in this month and in the previous one.
churn_next: the value of churn in the following month. This is the target that we want to predict.







Important



Our objective
Given a month (e.g., June), we want to use all the data up to the last day of the previous month (all months until May included) to predict whether a user will have churned as of July (i.e., their has_played flag will be False both in June and in July).
In other words, a row at month M means “act during month M, using data up to the end of M-1, to predict absence in M and M+1.”









Warning



Why we’re predicting one month in the future
Given the month of June, we may be tempted to use churn at this month as the target. However, June’s features are built from May, and churn for June is only true if the character is absent in May: any character that is active in May is labeled as “not churned” by construction, and the model would learn that just by looking at the missing values. This would produce overly optimistic results.
Shifting the target to July avoids this problem: in June we want to predict whether a player is active in July using data from and up to May.


One caveat with this modeling strategy is that we are working with historical data, so we cannot actually apply said incentive and observe whether it has an impact like in a typical A/B test.


We begin by adding two columns to the historical dataset: in the first we store each timestamp, truncated to have a monthly resolution; in the second we track the first month for each character. Additionally, we add a constant has_played column that acts as our “player was seen” flag.
We are interested in monthly snapshots, so the dataset is then reduced to select only the unique (character, month) pairs.






Data preparation


def make_data(df, interval="1mo"):
    """
    Prepare a dataframe that contains the months in which each player has
    actually played. The column "has_played" is then set to True for those months.
    Any month in which the player did not play is missing from this dataset,
    because the dataset is built starting from player activity, so any "empty
    month" simply doesn't exist in this dataset.
    """

    data = (
        df.with_columns(
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).alias("month"),
            first_month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).min().over("char"),
        )
        .unique(subset=["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(pl.lit(True).alias("has_played"))
    )
    return data

However, not all players will play at least once every month, so by relying exclusively on the historical data we would be missing samples; to get around this problem we generate a char_month dataset that contains all unique combinations of users and months by executing the cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.







Cross product
The cross product between two sets (in this case, months and unique users) builds a new set where each element in the first set is paired with all elements in the second set.

def make_user_month(df, interval="1mo"):
    """
    Create a DataFrame with all unique combinations of users and months.
    This will be used to ensure that we have a row for each user for each month
    in the range of the dataset, even if the user did not play in that month.

    This is done with a cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.

    This function is artificially generating 3 months past the last month in the
    dataset. Their "churn_next" is null, so `build_churn_dataset` drops them: they
    are only visible when calling `add_churn` directly.

    Note that since the months are generated from the range of the dataset, they
    may include months prior to a user's first activity. These will need to be
    filtered out later.
    """

    months = pl.datetime_range(
        start=df.select(pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).min())
        .collect()
        .item(),
        end=df.select(
            # Adding 3 months to the end of the range because we are adding
            # lagged features up to 3 months.
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).max().dt.offset_by("3mo")
        )
        .collect()
        .item(),
        interval=interval,
        closed="both",
        eager=True,
    )

    char_month = (
        df.with_columns(month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval))
        .select("char")
        .unique()
        .join(months.to_frame(name="month").lazy(), how="cross")
    )
    return char_month

Then we add the churn information. After sorting by month, prev_played is the has_played flag of the previous month for the same character (False for the first month), churn marks the characters absent in both months, and churn_next is churn shifted one month back within each character. The last observed month has no “next month” to look at, so its churn_next is left empty, and so is that of the three padding months.






Add the churn columns


def add_churn(user_month, data):
    """
    Add churn information to the user-month DataFrame by merging it with the actual
    play data. The resulting DataFrame will have a "has_played" column indicating
    whether the user played in that month. Any missing values in "has_played" are
    filled with False: missing values mean that the player did not play in that
    particular month.

    It also adds the "churn" column (churned as of this month: absent this month
    and the previous one) and the "churn_next" column, the prediction target:
    the value of "churn" in the *following* month. Features for a given month are
    built from the previous month's data, so the target cannot be the churn
    status of the same month: that status includes "absent last month", which
    is exactly what the features reveal. "churn_next" is null for the last
    observed month and for the padding months added by `make_user_month`,
    because the following month has not been observed.
    """

    last_month = data.lazy().select(pl.col("month").max()).collect().item()

    df_with_user_month = (
        user_month.join(
            data,
            on=["char", "month"],
            how="left",
        )
        .with_columns(pl.col("has_played").fill_null(False))
        .with_columns(first_month=pl.col("first_month").min().over("char"))
        .filter(pl.col("first_month") <= pl.col("month"))
        .select(
            "char",
            "month",
            "has_played",
            "first_month",
        )
        .sort(["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(
            # has_played in the previous month for this character
            prev_played=pl.col("has_played").shift(1).over("char").fill_null(False)
        )
        .with_columns(
            # churn = absent this month AND absent last month
            # prev_played is False on a character's first month
            churn=~pl.col("has_played") & ~pl.col("prev_played")
        )
        .with_columns(
            churn_next=pl.when(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo") <= last_month)
            .then(pl.col("churn").shift(-1).over("char"))
            .otherwise(None)
        )
        .select(
            "char",
            "month",
            "has_played",
            "prev_played",
            "churn",
            "churn_next",
            "first_month",
        )
    )
    return df_with_user_month

def build_churn_dataset(historical_data, only_prev_active=False):
    """
    Build the (char, month) table with `has_played`, `prev_played`, `churn` and
    the target `churn_next`.

    Rows whose target is unknown (the last observed month and the padding months
    after it) cannot be used to train or evaluate a model, so they are dropped.

    With `only_prev_active=True`, only the rows where the character played in the
    previous month are kept. Features for a row at month M are built from month
    M - 1, so a character that was already absent in M - 1 has no features and
    is not a prediction we could act on: the target then only contains
    characters that were active in M - 1 and are absent in both M and M + 1.
    Keep the default (all rows) when the full (char, month) grid is needed, for
    example to build lagged features, which need each character's full timeline.
    """
    # Load the dataset
    data = make_data(historical_data)
    # Add the combinations of user months
    user_month = make_user_month(historical_data)
    churn_data = add_churn(user_month, data).filter(
        pl.col("churn_next").is_not_null()
    )
    if only_prev_active:
        churn_data = churn_data.filter(pl.col("prev_played"))
    return churn_data.collect()

text:
2 A splitter that respects time
Before starting with feature engineering and actually training the model, it’s worth spending some time understanding the scenario we are in.
The main factor that complicates this scenario is the fact that we are dealing with sequential data points, which are therefore not independent of each other: the position of a player at a time T is strongly correlated with their position at time T+1.

2.1 Why the default splitter does not fit
For this reason, we need to use a splitter that returns sequential splits. A common example of this is scikit-learn’s TimeSeriesSplit. TimeSeriesSplit works by splitting the entire dataset in a given number of splits; during cross-validation, at step K the splitter returns the first k splits as the train split, and the k+1 split as the validation split.





Source
A downside of TimeSeriesSplit is that the splitter assumes uniformly distributed samples, so that each singular split has the same size as the others. This is a problem for our scenario: our samples are (character, month) pairs, and the number of characters in each month is never constant (in 2008, between about 6,700 and 12,500 rows per month):





For this reason, we need to define a custom splitter that is aware of the constraints we are working with. Given that we are working month-by-month, each split should contain all the rows of a specific month (the characters that played in the previous month, as explained above), and should be able to do so regardless of the fact that the number of characters changes.
There is a second constraint: the target of a row is the churn status of the following month, so it is only known one month later. If the training set included the rows of the month right before the test month, their targets would be computed from the activity in the test month. The splitter therefore leaves a one-month gap between the last training month and the test month.
This is what we implement here:


The boundaries of the experiment are defined in main.py: split points go from 2006-02-01 to 2008-10-01, and each test month is the one following its split point. The last test month is the latest one whose target is fully observed.




class Splitter:
    """
    Iterates over the months. For each split point, the test month is the
    following month: it is the month during which we would score users and act
    on the ones marked as "churn risks".

    The target of a row (churn_next) is the churn status of the month after it,
    so it is only known one month later. The training set therefore stops one
    month before the split point: a row from the split point month would have a
    target computed from the test month.
    """

    def split(self, user_month, has_played=None, interval="1mo"):
        # the target is not needed in this splitter since we are only splitting
        # based on the month
        del has_played
        time_range = pl.date_range(MIN_DATE, MAX_DATE, interval, eager=True)
        for split_point in time_range:
            # I can either use dateutils.relative delta
            # test_month = split_point + relativedelta(months=1)
            # Or do this with polars which is more consistent with the rest of the code
            test_month = pl.Series([split_point]).dt.offset_by(interval).first()
            last_train_month = (
                pl.Series([split_point]).dt.offset_by("-" + interval).first()
            )
            # Train indices are up to last_train_month, included
            train_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") <= last_train_month)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            # Test indices are for the month after split_point
            test_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") == test_month)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            if train_idx and test_idx:
                print(f"Working on month {split_point}")
                yield train_idx, test_idx

    def get_n_splits(self, X, y):
        return sum(1 for _ in self.split(X, y))


Like all other scikit-learn splitters, our splitter is a generator that, given X and y (user_month and the target in our case), returns the indices of the samples that should be used in each split.
With the target defined and the splits under control, the next part builds the features that describe each character’s month: sessions first, then location.

title: Part 4 · Location features, and whether they earn their place
text:
The previous section on sessionization modeled when a character is online, and their general time-specific behavior. This section focuses on answering where a character spends their time, as character location should be a signal of whether they are a dedicated player (focusing on late-game areas), or someone less committed to the game.
While generating these features originally appeared to be a promising direction, experimental results seem to show little to no impact on the actual prediction performance (see Does the block earn its place?). We keep the investigation for historical reasons, and to showcase a different application of the SessionEncoder.


To generate the features, we use again the SessionEncoder, split on (char, zone) instead of char:
session_encoder_zone = SessionEncoder(
    split_by=["char", "zone"],
    timestamp_col="timestamp",
    session_gap=session_gap * 60,
    suffix="session_id_zone",
)
A “zone session” is the interval between the first heartbeat in a zone, to the last one before they are seen somewhere else: this is a visit, not a play session. The two session IDs are independent and touch different columns, and a character’s sessions do not change whether or not the location features are enabled: this means that use_location can be a plain choose_bool.
Visits are much shorter than play sessions, because players move around inside a session. In March 2008, we measure ~385k zone sessions for 109k play sessions, and 49% of the visits consist of a single heartbeat.

title: Part 6 · Unseen data, runtime, and what the numbers mean
text:
3 Held-out evaluation on unseen files
The most distinctive part of the design is that the plan is fitted once and then run on files it has never seen, parsing included. Two windows make that work:

HISTORICAL_END = 2008-10-31 — everything up to and including October 2008 is training material.
UNSEEN_START = 2008-10-01 and UNSEEN_END = 2009-01-10 — the unseen window.

The two overlap by one month on purpose. November’s features are built from October’s activity, so if the unseen window started in November, the first month it could score would have no features at all. The overlap gives the unseen run one month of history to work from.
fit_final fits the whole graph — parsing included — on the historical files using every character, and saves the learner with joblib. score_unseen loads that saved learner and calls .predict() with the unseen environment. The same code path parses files it has never seen, which is the point: there is no separate pre-processing script that could drift from the training one.
Splitting the two matters because the fit is the expensive half. Once the learner is on disk, re-scoring is a load and a predict.

3.1 The result
Fitted on every character through October 2008, scored on November 2008:

That is below the 0.8817 the same configuration scores in cross-validation, and the gap is expected rather than a bug. The cross-validation number is a mean over 30 folds inside the historical window; this is a single month from a different period, and November’s churn rate (0.60) is far above the ~0.36 the model was trained around. A shifted base rate is exactly the situation where a ranking metric degrades.
The configuration is in reports/final_config.json and the fitted learner in reports/final_learner.joblib, so the run is reproducible without re-running the search.
January 2009 stops on the 10th because that is where the dataset ends. That caps the last usable target at December 2008 — a January row’s label would need February’s data to be observed — but December’s own label is churn in January, and a character who played on January 11th or later is recorded as absent. The label is therefore wrong for those characters, so the unseen evaluation reports November only.

4 Reading the execution report
Every evaluate() run writes a skrub report to reports/execution_report/. It is the easiest way to inspect the plan: the graph itself, per-node timing, and the fitted state of each transformer. Open reports/execution_report/index.html in a browser.
The node that dominates the runtime is the location block, which is why it is a choice rather than a fixed part of the plan.

title: Part 6 · Unseen data, runtime, and what the numbers mean
text:
5 Data quality and quirks
Several decisions in the code are responses to data problems that are easy to miss when reading the table:

guild == -1 means “no guild” and is mapped to null in make_data_op.
Duplicate heartbeats at the same timestamp exist, and show up as the 0s (duplicate) bar in the gap histogram.
The level cap moves: 60 → 70 in April 2007, 70 → 80 in November 2008. Any level-based feature is therefore not comparable across the whole window.
Expansion releases are a confounder: they cause both an influx of characters and a change in behaviour.

text:
6 Reproducing the post
The pixi tasks and the main.py CLI are the entry points:
# Evaluate the plan on the historical window
pixi run python main.py --env train --fraction 0.1

# Run one search stage
pixi run python main.py --env train --fraction 0.1 --stage capacity \
    --search --n-iter 60 --study-name wowah_churn_capacity \
    --frozen '{"session_gap": 60, "lags": [1,2,3], ...}'

# Fit on every character and save the learner
pixi run python main.py --env fit-final --fraction 1 \
    --frozen '{"session_gap": 60, "lags": [1,2,3], ...}'

# Load the saved learner and score November 2008
pixi run python main.py --env score-unseen
run_stages.py chains the stages, carrying each winner into the next:
pixi run python run_stages.py --stages gaps structural capacity
explore_data.py regenerates the exploration figures. Determinism is partial: sample_by_user uses seed=42, but the model is not seeded, so AUC varies by a few hundredths between runs. With the parquet source a 10% trial takes about two minutes; the full-data fit takes about the same, because the parse is no longer the bottleneck.
The search runs sequentially. Parallel trials are not offered: parsing spawns a process pool sized to the core count, so N workers on a cold cache means N × cores processes, and eight workers drove a 24 GB machine into 40 GB of swap.

title: Part 6 · Unseen data, runtime, and what the numbers mean
text:
7 Caching the plan
Parsing the raw logs is the most expensive thing in the project, and the way the pipeline is evaluated makes it worse than it looks. This section is about the one line of configuration that fixes it, and about the trap that makes the fix dangerous if you forget it.

7.1 The parse is a node, and the node runs 63 times
load is not a preprocessing step that happens before the pipeline starts. It is a node of the plan, sitting at the top of the graph:
raw_files = skrub.var("raw_files")
historical_data = raw_files.skb.apply_func(load, fraction=load_fraction)
That is deliberate — it is what lets the same graph be fitted on the historical files and later run on files it has never seen. But it also means the parse is re-executed every time the plan is evaluated, and cross_validate evaluates the plan once per fit and once per score:
\[30 \text{ folds} \times 2 + 1 = 61 \text{ evaluations}\]
Each evaluation parses all 138,084 historical heartbeat files. A single parse takes 68 s and returns 36.5M rows, so an uncached cross-validation spends about 69 minutes parsing alone — before any feature engineering or model fitting.


7.2 One line turns it off
skrub’s Data Ops cache is a single configuration call:
CACHE_DIR = Path(__file__).parent / ".skrub_cache"
skrub.set_config(cache=str(CACHE_DIR))
With it on, the first evaluation parses and every later one reuses the result. Measured end to end at load_fraction=0.1:




wall time

The cache-off figure is extrapolated rather than measured: an uncached cross_validate was still running after 30 minutes and was stopped. The 61-call count and the 68 s per-call cost were both measured directly, by memoizing the parse so the count could be taken without paying 61 × 68 s.


7.3 Two different savings, often confused
The table hides two separate effects, and they are not the same size:

cache off → cache on: 63 parses become 1. About 15× faster. This is the one that matters.
cache cold → cache warm: 1 parse becomes 0. 289 s → 213 s, about 26%. Modest, because the remaining time is model fitting and encoding, not parsing.

So “the cache makes the run 26% faster” is true and misleading. The cache is the difference between a run you can iterate on and a run you leave overnight. The 26% is what you get on the second run of the day.


7.4 The trap: the cache does not know your code changed
joblib keys a cached call on the cached function’s own source plus its arguments. It does not look at the functions that function calls. So editing adding_features.py would leave build_feature_table’s cache key unchanged, and the cache would keep serving the old feature table — silently, with no warning, and with results that look plausible.
The workaround is to put the dependency back into the key by passing a source fingerprint as an extra argument:
def _source_fingerprint(*modules):
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    for module in modules:
        digest.update(Path(module.__file__).read_bytes())
    return digest.hexdigest()[:16]


FEATURES_FINGERPRINT = _source_fingerprint(
    sys.modules[__name__],
    sys.modules["add_churn"],
    sys.modules["adding_features"],
)
build_feature_table accepts _fingerprint=None and immediately does del _fingerprint: the argument exists only to change the cache key, and never reaches the computation.

The parse node is deliberately left out. The parser is frozen, so the guard would only ever fire on a change that is not going to happen — and the cost of leaving it out is that editing src/parse_to_single_table.py is not detected. That is a tidiness trade-off, not a correctness one: delete .skrub_cache/ by hand if you ever change the parser.
If you add a module that build_feature_table calls, add it to the _source_fingerprint(...) call. Otherwise edits to it will be ignored.


7.5 What the cache costs
The cache directory is 587 MB and git-ignored. It is regenerated on demand, so deleting it is always safe — it just costs a full recompute, which is the ~75 minutes above. That is the price of changing the parser, or of clearing the cache to be sure you are not looking at stale features.


7.6 The unseen environment gets its own entry
The cache is keyed on the arguments of the cached call, and raw_files is one of them. The training and unseen environments pass different file lists, so they get separate cache entries and neither invalidates the other.
The unseen set is much smaller — 10,058 files, 2.31M rows, 7.3 s to parse — so caching matters far less there. fit_final fits on the historical files and then parses the unseen ones once; the cache saves that single parse on a repeat run and nothing more.


7.7 Skipping the parse entirely
Caching makes the parse happen once. Reading a pre-parsed file makes it happen never, and that is what the searches actually use.
build_parquet.py writes the whole corpus to data/wowah_data_all.parquet by calling parse_files itself, so the two cannot drift. make_data_op then takes a source argument: "parquet" reads that file, "raw" parses the .txt files. Both go through the same code, so the choice does not change any result.

section: 8 Limitations and what would come next
text:
8 Limitations and what would come next

Right-censoring. Characters still active at the end of the window have no observed churn, and the last months are dropped entirely. A survival-analysis framing (time-to-churn) would use those rows instead of throwing them away.
Avatars are treated as players. A player with several avatars is counted several times, and churn on one avatar is not churn on the player.
No causal claim. The model says who is at risk, not whether an incentive would have worked.
Monthly granularity is a choice. Weekly would give more folds but a noisier label.
